title: Top-K Ranking
explain: Top-K ranking returns the `k` best items out of `n` by score without sorting everything. The trick is a size-`k` **min**-heap whose root is the current k-th best, so almost every new item is rejected by one comparison. It costs `O(n log k)` time and `O(k)` memory and works on a stream. (小顶堆守门: the weakest of the winners guards the door.)
model:
Keep the best `k` seen so far in a **min**-heap. The root is the *cutoff*, the k-th best.

```
for each score s:
    if heap.size < k:     push(s)
    elif s > heap.root:   replace root with s, sift down
    else:                 discard
```

| Option | Time | Memory | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sort everything | `O(n log n)` | `O(n)` | small `n`, or you need the full order |
| Min-heap of size `k` | `O(n log k)` | `O(k)` | streams, large `n` |
| Quickselect | `O(n)` average | `O(n)` | all data in memory, order inside the top-k not needed |

**Distributed:** every shard returns its *local* top-k and a coordinator merges the lists (again with a heap). The global top-k is always inside the union of the local top-k lists, so each shard must return at least `k`.

The score itself usually comes from [weighted event scoring](#/sd/f/weighted-event-scoring).

details.q: Why a min-heap and not a max-heap?
details.a: You need the *cutoff* handy, and the cutoff is the smallest of the current winners. A min-heap exposes exactly that at the root, so one comparison decides whether a new item can enter. A max-heap keeps the wrong end handy and would force you to hold or scan everything.

Top 3 of the stream 5, 1, 8, 3, 9, 2, 7. The heap fills with {1, 5, 8}. Then 3 beats the root 1 (now {3, 5, 8}), 9 beats 3 ({5, 8, 9}), 2 is discarded, 7 beats 5 ({7, 8, 9}). Three replacements, and most items in a long stream behave like the discarded 2.

details.q: Each of 8 shards holds part of the catalogue. What must a shard return for a correct global top-10?
details.a: At least its own top 10. In the worst case all ten global winners live on one shard, so returning `10/8` per shard can drop true winners. The coordinator merges 8 sorted lists of 10 and keeps the best 10.

details.q: Why is deep pagination ('page 1,000') expensive, and what do you do instead?
details.a: Page `N` of size `s` needs the top `N*s` from every shard, then a merge that throws most of it away, so the work grows with the offset times the number of shards. Use a cursor (the last score and id seen) so each page asks for 'the next `s` after this key'.

details.q: Two items tie for 5th place and the page flickers between them. Fix?
details.a: Ranking needs a total order. Add a deterministic tie-breaker such as the item id as a secondary sort key, so the same input always gives the same output. Random tie-breaking is only right if fairness between ties is a deliberate product choice.

details.q: The scores change over time. Does a heap still work?
details.a: Not directly: a heap has no cheap 'update this item's score'. Either recompute periodically over a window, keep per-bucket counters ([time-bucket counters](#/sd/f/time-bucket-counter), [sliding windows](#/sd/f/sliding-window-aggregation)) and rebuild the top-k from them, or use an indexed heap or sorted structure if you really need point updates.

details.q: How do you find the top-k most frequent items in a huge stream?
details.a: Counting everything is too big, so pair an approximate counter such as a count-min sketch (frequency estimates in small memory) with a size-`k` heap of the current heavy hitters. Estimates only over-count, so confirm the final candidates with an exact pass if precision matters.

prompts.q: Explain top-k ranking and why you would not just sort.
points: Top-k returns the k best of n by score
Sorting is O(n log n) and holds everything
Min-heap of size k: root is the cutoff, one comparison per item
O(n log k) time, O(k) memory, works on a stream
Quickselect as the in-memory O(n) alternative

prompts.q: Describe top-k over a sharded catalogue, including pagination.
points: Each shard returns its local top-k, at least k
Coordinator merges lists with a heap
Global top-k lies inside the union of local top-k
Deep offsets cost shards x offset, so use cursors

prompts.q: Design a trending list where scores keep changing.
points: Score comes from weighted, decayed events
A heap cannot update cheaply, so bucket by time or recompute on a window
Approximate counting (count-min) plus a heap for heavy hitters
